power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

table.expanded: The resulting model showed very good fit, χ²[13] = 15.67, p = .268, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .01, SRMR = .01.

For the latent change score model of the learningoriented factor, three of 12 threshold equality constraints had to be freed to achieve partial measurement invariance, resulting in very good model fit, χ²[13] = 15.88, p = .256, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .01, SRMR = .01.

For the task-completion factor, four of 16 threshold equality constraints had to be freed to achieve partial measurement invariance, again resulting in very good model fit, χ²[24] = 31.47, p = .141, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .01, SRMR = .01.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .268", "p = .256", "p = .141"), Sentence = c("The resulting model showed very good fit, χ²[13] = 15.67, p = .268, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .01, SRMR = .01.", "For the latent change score model of the learningoriented factor, three of 12 threshold equality constraints had to be freed to achieve partial measurement invariance, resulting in very good model fit, χ²[13] = 15.88, p = .256, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .01, SRMR = .01.", "For the task-completion factor, four of 16 threshold equality constraints had to be freed to achieve partial measurement invariance, again resulting in very good model fit, χ²[24] = 31.47, p = .141, CFI = 1.00, TLI = 1.00, RMSEA = .01, SRMR = .01." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Self-Directed Generative AI Use and Academic Development Among Secondary School Students: A Large-Scale, One-Year Longitudinal Study

text.text: Teacher Education at the University of Bonn.
We have no known conflicts of interest to declare.
Example code can be found in Supplement S2.

Generative AI tools (ChatGPT, OpenAI; Claude, Anthropic) were used for copyediting and document quality control, including checks for consistency in terminology, headings, cross-references, and table and figure labels, as well as to assist in drafting and checking Mplus analysis code.
All AIgenerated suggestions and AI-assisted code were reviewed, tested where applicable, and validated by the authors, who take full responsibility for the final manuscript.

Students' self-directed use of generative AI (GenAI) tools for schoolwork is increasing rapidly, and this study found that students with lower achievement at the beginning of the school year reported using GenAI more often at the end of the year, whereas earlier GenAI use did not predict later achievement.

Considering both types of use together, students who used GenAI more often to get tasks done reported investing less effort by the end of the school year in four of six subjects, whereas those who used it more often to learn tended to report more effort.
Guidance on using GenAI for learning may therefore be particularly important, especially for lower-achieving students.

The widespread availability of generative AI (GenAI) tools, such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, is transforming how students learn and how teachers prepare and teach in schools and classrooms (Chiu, 2024; Giannakos et al., 2025).

text.text: Likewise, research on the antecedents of self-directed GenAI use in educational contexts is only beginning to emerge (Granić, 2025; Nguyen et al., 2026).

text.text: This gap is particularly striking given the intense societal debates surrounding potential effects of selfdirected GenAI use and its growing prevalence among students (e.g., Baek et al., 2024; Darvishi et al., 2024; Kasneci et al., 2023; New York City Mayor's Office, 2026; Panadero & Broadbent, 2025; Yan et al., 2024).

text.text: Prior research suggests that it is not GenAI use per se, but rather the purpose for which and the way in which GenAI is used that is critical to understanding its relation to achievement, motivation, and effort (e.g., Y. Chen et al., 2026; Giannakos et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025; Panadero & Broadbent, 2025; Weidlich et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2024).

text.text: For instance, theoretical work has argued that GenAI systems may differentially support or undermine learning depending on whether they increase or reduce cognitive engagement (Acemoglu et al., 2026).

text.text: Related to this, decades of educational psychology research have shown that motivation-an important educational outcome (Jansen et al., 2022) and predictor of later academic achievement and choices (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002 , 2020)-is closely linked to active engagement and effort during learning processes.

text.text: Thus, integrating theoretical and empirical insights from research on motivation and GenAI in education suggests that students' patterns of self-directed GenAI use may both shape and be shaped by students' effort, motivation, and academic achievement over time (e.g., Panadero & Broadbent, 2025).

text.text: To date, large-scale longitudinal studies examining reciprocal associations between selfdirected GenAI use and students' academic achievement, motivation, and effort in naturalistic school settings remain scarce, leaving these associations poorly understood.

To address this gap, we conducted a secondary analysis of longitudinal data from the TOSCAneo study, comprising 4,062 students from 136 secondary schools in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, surveyed at the beginning and end of the 2023/2024 school year (Schnaufer et al., 2026a (Schnaufer et al., , 2026b)).
text.formatted: To address this gap, we conducted a secondary analysis of longitudinal data from the TOSCAneo study, comprising 4,062 students from 136 secondary schools in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, surveyed at the beginning and end of the 2023/2024 school year <ref type="bibr">(Schnaufer et al., 2026a</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Schnaufer et al., , 2026b))</ref>.

text.text: Our study design has three key features: First, we measured achievement with standardized tests rather than self-reported grades.
Second, we captured students' self-directed GenAI use, rather than assigning or experimentally inducing it.
Third, we assessed achievement, self-concept, value beliefs, and effort at both time points in six subjects, which allowed us to estimate associations with GenAI use in both directions.
With this design, we move beyond asking whether GenAI use helps or harms students on average.
Instead, we examine which forms of self-directed use relate to students' achievement, motivation, and effort, and which students turn to GenAI in the first place.
This offers a level of specificity that is currently lacking in the debate about the effects of students' self-directed GenAI use on their academic development.

Theories of learning emphasize that knowledge acquisition depends on learners' active cognitive engagement with tasks and learning materials, including processes such as elaboration, explanation, and the integration of new information with prior knowledge (e.g., Chi & Wylie, 2014; Fiorella & Mayer, 2015; Freeman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Theories of learning emphasize that knowledge acquisition depends on learners' active cognitive engagement with tasks and learning materials, including processes such as elaboration, explanation, and the integration of new information with prior knowledge (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Chi & Wylie, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Fiorella & Mayer, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Freeman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These engagement processes may be altered when GenAI is used for a task (e.g., Cho, 2026).
text.formatted: These engagement processes may be altered when GenAI is used for a task (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Cho, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Through active cognitive engagement, learners are more likely to develop coherent, transferable, and wellstructured knowledge representations.
Conversely, when cognitive engagement is reduced, opportunities for meaningful learning and skill development may become limited.

Prior educational research suggests that students can approach academic tasks with different goals and intentions, which influence how they engage with learning activities and regulate their effort (Ames, 1992; Elliott & Dweck, 1988).
text.formatted: Prior educational research suggests that students can approach academic tasks with different goals and intentions, which influence how they engage with learning activities and regulate their effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Ames, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Elliott & Dweck, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: Drawing on these perspectives, the effects of students' self-directed GenAI use may differ depending on whether GenAI is primarily used to facilitate task completion or to support understanding and learning.

When GenAI is used to complete academic tasks efficiently, students may offload substantial parts of cognitive work to the system, thereby reducing active cognitive engagement with the learning material (Fan et al., 2025; Stadler et al., 2024).
text.formatted: When GenAI is used to complete academic tasks efficiently, students may offload substantial parts of cognitive work to the system, thereby reducing active cognitive engagement with the learning material <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Fan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Stadler et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: GenAI may make this form of task completion particularly accessible because academic outputs can increasingly be produced with comparatively little effort or active processing.
In such cases, GenAI use may reduce opportunities for practice, elaboration, and knowledge construction.
In contrast, GenAI can also be used in ways that support active learning processes.
For example, students may use GenAI for learning-oriented purposes, such as obtaining explanations, clarifying concepts, generating examples, or supporting exam preparation.
In these cases, GenAI use may promote rather than reduce cognitive engagement by supporting elaboration and deeper processing of learning materials (J. Lee et al., 2025; Xiao et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In these cases, GenAI use may promote rather than reduce cognitive engagement by supporting elaboration and deeper processing of learning materials (J. <ref type="bibr">Lee et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Xiao et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, the educational consequences of GenAI use may depend less on whether students use GenAI and more on the purpose for which GenAI is used during academic activities.

Forms of use that are focused on task completion may contribute to reduced motivation and effort and, potentially, to deskilling over time (Stadler et al., 2024), whereas learning-oriented use may support effort and skill development (Xiao et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Forms of use that are focused on task completion may contribute to reduced motivation and effort and, potentially, to deskilling over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Stadler et al., 2024)</ref>, whereas learning-oriented use may support effort and skill development <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Xiao et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Student GenAI use might also play a pivotal role in developing academic motivation and effort.
According to (situated) expectancy-value theories (e.g., Atkinson, 1957; Eccles & Wigfield, 2020), students' expectancy and value beliefs represent central motivational drivers of academic behavior.
text.formatted: According to (situated) expectancy-value theories (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Atkinson, 1957;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>, students' expectancy and value beliefs represent central motivational drivers of academic behavior.

text.text: Expectancy beliefs reflect students' perceptions of their competence and likelihood of success, whereas value beliefs capture the perceived importance, usefulness, or intrinsic interest of a task (e.g., Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: Expectancy beliefs reflect students' perceptions of their competence and likelihood of success, whereas value beliefs capture the perceived importance, usefulness, or intrinsic interest of a task (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Together, these beliefs shape students' willingness to invest effort, persist in challenging activities, and actively engage in learning processes (e.g., Eccles & Wigfield, 2000).
text.formatted: Together, these beliefs shape students' willingness to invest effort, persist in challenging activities, and actively engage in learning processes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Eccles & Wigfield, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Academic effort can therefore be understood as a behavioral manifestation or indicator of students' underlying motivation.
Sustained effort, in turn, is considered an important prerequisite for long-term skill development and academic achievement.

Therefore, in line with prior studies (e.g., Gaspard et al., 2016), we consider self-concept and value beliefs as theory-based aspects of academic motivation and effort as a behavioral consequence of motivation.

text.text: Different forms of GenAI use may have distinct implications for students' academic motivation and willingness to invest effort in future learning activities.

Forms of GenAI use in which GenAI is primarily used to complete tasks efficiently or replace cognitive work may reduce the perceived necessity and value of exerting effort during learning activities (Fan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Forms of GenAI use in which GenAI is primarily used to complete tasks efficiently or replace cognitive work may reduce the perceived necessity and value of exerting effort during learning activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Fan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: If students repeatedly experience that academic tasks can be completed successfully with minimal cognitive engagement, effort itself may become perceived as less important or less worthwhile (e.g., Jansen et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: If students repeatedly experience that academic tasks can be completed successfully with minimal cognitive engagement, effort itself may become perceived as less important or less worthwhile (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Jansen et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Yan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the same vein, students might feel they will not be able to perform as well as the AI, potentially undermining learners' subject-specific self-concept (Jansen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In the same vein, students might feel they will not be able to perform as well as the AI, potentially undermining learners' subject-specific self-concept <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Jansen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, this may reduce students' willingness to engage actively, persist in cognitively demanding tasks, and exert effort (H.-P. Lee et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Over time, this may reduce students' willingness to engage actively, persist in cognitively demanding tasks, and exert effort (H.-P. <ref type="bibr">Lee et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, when GenAI is used to support rather than replace cognitive processes, it may foster learners' perceptions of competence while still requiring active effort and engagement.

For example, GenAI-supported explanations, feedback, or scaffolding may help students successfully engage with challenging tasks without bypassing the underlying learning processes (Fütterer et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For example, GenAI-supported explanations, feedback, or scaffolding may help students successfully engage with challenging tasks without bypassing the underlying learning processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Fütterer et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In line with expectancy-value frameworks (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020), such experiences of competence and successful engagement may support motivation and sustained effort in future learning activities.
text.formatted: In line with expectancy-value frameworks <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>, such experiences of competence and successful engagement may support motivation and sustained effort in future learning activities.

text.text: Emerging empirical evidence supports the assumption that GenAI use may have motivational consequences; however, the direction of effects seems mostly negative.
This is in line with hypotheses laid out by Fan et al. (2026).

text.text: For example, G. Liu et al. (2026) found that although GenAI assistance improved short-term task performance, participants subsequently performed worse without GenAI support and were more likely to give up on challenging tasks, indicative of reduced motivation and effort. Mei et al. (2025) found in a university context that learners were able to improve their text quality when using GenAI in a creative writing task but reported it was less enjoyable and valuable.

text.text: These findings suggest that certain forms of GenAI use may negatively affect not only performance but also motivation, task persistence, and willingness to exert effort during learning activities (see also H.-P. Lee et al., 2025).

text.text: Overall, while evidence is emerging, longitudinal studies of selfdirected GenAI use in K-12 contexts that distinguish between different ways of using GenAI and consider academic outcomes are still missing in the context of self-directed AI use (see Fütterer et al., 2026, for studies on GenAI-driven interventions).

text.text: Students' prior achievement might also influence how they engage with GenAI because productive use requires students to formulate appropriate queries, evaluate generated outputs, and integrate them with their existing knowledge.
These processes depend on prior knowledge and subject-specific competencies (Alexander, 1992; Dochy et al., 1999), and the related capacity to regulate one's own learning (e.g., Zimmerman, 2000).

text.text: Given the positive association between academic achievement and self-regulated learning (Dent & Koenka, 2016), higher-achieving students may therefore be better positioned to evaluate whether and how GenAI use serves their longer-term learning goals and to use GenAI in ways that effectively support their own learning processes (X. Xu et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Given the positive association between academic achievement and self-regulated learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dent & Koenka, 2016)</ref>, higher-achieving students may therefore be better positioned to evaluate whether and how GenAI use serves their longer-term learning goals and to use GenAI in ways that effectively support their own learning processes (X. <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Xu et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Yang et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, they may be more likely to recognize when using GenAI to generate an answer would replace learning-relevant cognitive activity and instead use it to obtain explanations, clarify concepts, or support their own problem-solving.

In contrast, lower-achieving students may face a double disadvantage: greater need for immediate assistance with academic tasks while simultaneously having fewer cognitive and self-regulatory resources to use GenAI in ways that support longer-term learning.

Prior achievement may therefore shape not only students' need for GenAI assistance, but also their capacity to use such assistance strategically, potentially contributing to greater task-completion use among lower-achieving students and greater learning-oriented use among higher-achieving students.
Students' academic motivation and effort may also shape how they use GenAI during academic tasks.

According to expectancy-value theory, students' decisions about whether and how strongly to engage in academic activities depend on their expectations of success and the value they attach to these activities (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).
text.formatted: According to expectancy-value theory, students' decisions about whether and how strongly to engage in academic activities depend on their expectations of success and the value they attach to these activities <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: These motivational beliefs may therefore also influence whether students use GenAI primarily as a means of completing academic tasks or as a resource for learning (e.g., Pan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These motivational beliefs may therefore also influence whether students use GenAI primarily as a means of completing academic tasks or as a resource for learning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">Pan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Situated expectancy-value theory (Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) implies that students with lower academic self-concept in a subject would be particularly likely to use GenAI to complete academic tasks when they perceive themselves as less capable of successfully completing them independently.
text.formatted: Situated expectancy-value theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref> implies that students with lower academic self-concept in a subject would be particularly likely to use GenAI to complete academic tasks when they perceive themselves as less capable of successfully completing them independently.

text.text: In such situations, GenAI provides an accessible way to obtain solutions or produce academic outputs while reducing the demands placed on the learner.
Similarly, students who perceive little value in an academic task may have fewer reasons to invest substantial cognitive effort in completing it themselves (Fan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Similarly, students who perceive little value in an academic task may have fewer reasons to invest substantial cognitive effort in completing it themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Fan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Using GenAI to facilitate task completion may therefore be particularly attractive when students consider an activity uninteresting, unimportant, or of little utility.
Finally, students who generally tend to invest less effort in academic activities may be more inclined to use GenAI in ways that minimize the effort required for task completion.

Thus, situated expectancy-value theory (e.g., Eccles & Wigfield, 2020) would predict greater taskcompletion GenAI use among students with lower subject-specific self-concept, value beliefs, and tendency to exert academic effort in a subject.
text.formatted: Thus, situated expectancy-value theory (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Eccles & Wigfield, 2020)</ref> would predict greater taskcompletion GenAI use among students with lower subject-specific self-concept, value beliefs, and tendency to exert academic effort in a subject.

text.text: Conversely, stronger academic motivation may be associated with greater learningoriented GenAI use.

Students who value learning activities and are willing to invest effort may be more likely to use GenAI in ways that support their own learning processes (e.g., Wang et al., 2026), for example, by requesting explanations, generating examples, or preparing for exams or tests.
text.formatted: Students who value learning activities and are willing to invest effort may be more likely to use GenAI in ways that support their own learning processes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Wang et al., 2026)</ref>, for example, by requesting explanations, generating examples, or preparing for exams or tests.

text.text: Students with stronger academic self-concepts tend to show more adaptive engagement with academic tasks, including greater persistence and willingness to invest effort in learning (Eccles & Wigfield, 2002; Marsh & Craven, 2006).
text.formatted: Students with stronger academic self-concepts tend to show more adaptive engagement with academic tasks, including greater persistence and willingness to invest effort in learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Eccles & Wigfield, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Marsh & Craven, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: They may therefore be more likely to approach GenAI as an additional learning resource rather than as a substitute for their own cognitive activity.
From this perspective, students' motivation may shape not only whether they engage with GenAI, but also the purposes for which they use it.
These relations may contribute to reciprocal dynamics between GenAI use and academic motivation and effort.

If lower academic motivation increases task-completion GenAI use, and task-completion GenAI use subsequently reduces students' willingness to invest effort in academic activities, initial motivational differences may be reinforced over time.
Likewise, learning-oriented GenAI use and stronger academic motivation may mutually reinforce one another.

Examining these reciprocal relationships is thus central to improving our understanding of how different forms of GenAI use and key academic variables, such as achievement, motivation, and effort, co-develop over time.

As outlined above, empirical research on students' self-directed use of GenAI and its reciprocal relations with academic achievement, motivation, and effort remains limited, particularly in naturalistic school contexts.

Much of the existing evidence relies on selfreported achievement outcomes (e.g., Gerlich, 2025; J. Lee et al., 2025), focuses on adult learners (e.g., H.-P. text.text: Understanding how students use GenAI in the absence of system-led prompting or instructor guidance is particularly important because these tools are continuously available to learners and are likely to be used under authentic, self-directed conditions.

The present study addresses this gap by examining secondary school students' self-directed GenAI use across an entire school year, considering a rich set of academic outcomes (i.e., achievement, self-concept, value beliefs, and effort) in six subjects.

Importantly, we distinguish between taskcompletion and learning-oriented forms of GenAI use as qualitatively different patterns of engagement that may differentially shape skill development, motivation, and effort.

Specifically, we address the following research question: How do secondary school students' task-completion and learning-oriented uses of GenAI tools relate reciprocally to their academic achievement, self-concept, value beliefs, and effort over the course of a school year across six subjects?

Addressing this question has important implications not only for understanding what predicts self-directed GenAI use and how this form of GenAI use is related to subsequent achievement, motivation, and effort, but also for the development of interventions and guidance that distinguish between forms of GenAI use that support versus undermine learning-oriented cognitive and motivational processes.

Based on the theoretical considerations outlined above, we hypothesized that learning-oriented GenAI use would be positively associated with future academic achievement, motivation, and effort, whereas taskcompletion GenAI use would be negatively associated with these outcomes over time.

Similarly, we hypothesized that students' academic motivation (i.e., subject-specific selfconcept and value beliefs), academic effort as a behavioral manifestation of motivation, and academic achievement would predict subsequent GenAI use.

Specifically, students with higher academic motivation, greater prior effort, and higher academic achievement were expected to engage more frequently in learning-oriented GenAI use and less frequently in task-completion GenAI use than students with lower motivation, effort, and achievement.

Students' GenAI tool use for academic purposes was assessed with seven items describing different academic activities: "solving tasks during class", "preparing for exams or tests", "doing homework", "preparing presentations and essays", "better understanding of class material", "further learning", and "translating texts".

Students rated how often they engaged in each activity on a 5-point response scale scored 0 (never), 1 (less than once a month), 2 (at least once a month but not every week), 3 (at least once a week but not every school day), and 4 (every school day).
We grouped the items into a task-completion factor and a learning-oriented factor of self-directed GenAI use.

The task-completion GenAI factor consisted of four items capturing task-completion use (i.e., using GenAI for "translating texts", "doing homework", "preparing presentations and essays", and "solving tasks during class"), whereas the learning-oriented GenAI factor consisted of three items capturing learning-oriented use (i.e., using GenAI for "better understanding of class material", "further learning", and "preparing for exams or tests"; see Supplement S2: Mplus Code A).

text.text: The analysis followed two major steps: First, we examined the different items related to GenAI tool use for academic purposes and the changes between T1 and T2.

This was done by estimating means of the latent response variable (y*) in an IRT framework for each of the seven GenAI items at T1 and T2 and comparing these means using the delta method implemented in the model constraint options in Mplus (Ver Hoef, 2012), cluster-robust standard errors, and survey weights (see Supplement S2: Mplus Code B).

In addition, we estimated latent change score models for task-completion GenAI use (T) and learning-oriented GenAI use (L), with the T1 latent variance fixed to 1 so that the average latent change could be interpreted in SD units of T1 (see Supplement S2: Mplus Code C).

Second, considering the reciprocal associations between GenAI use and academic outcomes, we specified a cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) that included the six latent variables of interest at T1 (i.e., task-completion GenAI use, learning-oriented GenAI use, academic achievement, self-concept, value beliefs, and effort) and the same set of latent variables at T2 (see Supplement S2: Mplus Code D for exemplary code).

text.text: For mathematics, science subjects, and German, this was true for both learning-oriented and task-completion GenAI use.
In English, there was only a statistically significant association with taskcompletion GenAI use, but not with learning-oriented GenAI use.

These findings suggest that students with lower achievement at the beginning of the school year reported using GenAI more often by the end of the school year for learning-oriented and task-completion purposes, after controlling for all other variables at T1.

Considering reciprocal associations between prior GenAI use and later self-concept, we found only one positive association, namely prior task-completion GenAI use predicting later self-concept in mathematics (β = .17, p = .013).

In addition, we found a positive association between prior self-concept and later task-completion GenAI use in chemistry (β = .15, p = .006), but no statistically significant associations in any of the other subjects.

When examining associations between prior GenAI use and value beliefs, we found a negative association between task-completion GenAI use and later value beliefs (β = -.21, p = .049) and a positive association between learning-oriented GenAI use and later value beliefs (β = .22, p = .020) in physics.

The difference between these two coefficients was statistically significant (p = .035), implying that students with higher learning-oriented GenAI use at T1 reported higher value beliefs at T2, whereas students with higher task-completion use reported lower value beliefs at T2.

When examining the predictive effects of prior value beliefs on GenAI use, we found that prior value beliefs in mathematics were positively associated with subsequent learningoriented GenAI use (β = .12, p = .049), whereas there was no statistically significant association with task-completion GenAI use.

In addition, negative associations were found between prior value beliefs in chemistry and both subsequent task-completion (β = -.17, p = .006) and learning-oriented (β = -.16, p = .008) GenAI use, as well as with task-completion GenAI use in biology (β = -.17, p = .021).
These findings suggest that students with lower value beliefs at the beginning of the school year tended to use GenAI more often in chemistry and biology by the end of the school year.
For German and English, we did not find any statistically significant associations between prior value beliefs and subsequent GenAI use after controlling for the other variables in the model at T1.
Finally, we examined reciprocal relations between GenAI use and effort.

Regarding paths from prior GenAI use to later effort, we found a negative association for taskcompletion GenAI use in mathematics (β = -.24, p = .002), in chemistry (β = -.25, p = .003), in physics (β = -.42, p < .001), and in English (β = -.25, p = .008), whereas there was a positive association between prior learning-oriented GenAI use and subsequent effort in mathematics (β = .21, p = .011), chemistry (β = .19, p = .023), and physics (β = .39, p < .001).

text.text: The present study examined reciprocal relationships between students' self-directed task-completion and learning-oriented GenAI use and the development of academic achievement, motivation, and effort across one school year.
Two main patterns emerged: First, a GenAI use profile weighted toward task completion rather than learning predicted lower subsequent effort.
The difference between the task-completion and learning-oriented coefficients was statistically significant in mathematics, chemistry, physics, and English.
Interestingly, with regard to the direction of the coefficients, a similar pattern was observed for value beliefs.
However, this pattern was statistically significant only in physics.
In contrast, we found little evidence that either form of GenAI use systematically predicted subsequent academic achievement or self-concept.

Second, in the reverse direction, prior achievement consistently predicted subsequent GenAI use, with higher-achieving students reporting less frequent task-completion and learning-oriented use and lower-achieving students reporting more frequent task-completion and learning-oriented use.
Associations of prior motivational beliefs and effort with subsequent GenAI use were comparatively small and inconsistent.
Together, these findings provide a nuanced picture of the reciprocal relationships between students' GenAI use and their academic development over the course of the school year.

For academic effort, in line with expectations, we found that students reporting more task-completion GenAI use showed lower effort in the respective subject by the end of the school year, whereas students reporting more learning-oriented GenAI use showed higher subsequent effort.

These findings are consistent with the assumption that the educational consequences of GenAI use may depend less on whether students use GenAI and more on the purpose for which GenAI is used during academic activities (e.g., Y. Chen et al., 2026; Giannakos et al., 2025; Han et al., 2025; Panadero & Broadbent, 2025; Weidlich et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2024).

text.text: From a theoretical perspective, one possible explanation for this pattern concerns differences in learners' cognitive engagement when interacting with GenAI.

Task-completion forms of GenAI use may reduce the need for learners to engage in retrieval, elaboration, or problem solving by shifting parts of the cognitive work to the GenAI system (Risko & Gilbert, 2016).
text.formatted: Task-completion forms of GenAI use may reduce the need for learners to engage in retrieval, elaboration, or problem solving by shifting parts of the cognitive work to the GenAI system <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Risko & Gilbert, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, learning-oriented uses may support active processing when GenAI is used to obtain explanations or feedback or to facilitate reflection and elaboration (Chi & Wylie, 2014; Fiorella & Mayer, 2015).
text.formatted: In contrast, learning-oriented uses may support active processing when GenAI is used to obtain explanations or feedback or to facilitate reflection and elaboration <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Chi & Wylie, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Fiorella & Mayer, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The observed differences in subsequent effort are therefore consistent with theoretical perspectives emphasizing that technologies can either reduce or support active engagement depending on how learners interact with them.
More broadly, these findings illustrate why treating GenAI use as a unitary construct may obscure meaningful differences in students' interactions with these systems.

This interpretation should take into account the strong correlation between the two GenAI factors (r = .86 at T1 and .81 at T2), which exceeds the stability of either factor across the school year (.62 and .51).
Because the two forms of GenAI use were strongly correlated and entered simultaneously, their coefficients reflect associations with later effort conditional on the other form of use.

The similar-magnitude, opposite-sign coefficients therefore suggest that differences in the relative composition of GenAI use may have been more relevant to later effort than students' overall level of use.

This interpretation is also broadly consistent with the achievement results: both forms of GenAI use were predicted by prior achievement in the same direction, with overlapping confidence intervals, suggesting that lower-achieving students tended to report greater use of both forms rather than a clearly different balance between them.
Whether the two forms of use would show the same pattern if assessed with items designed to distinguish them more sharply remains an open question.
At the same time, the present data cannot establish the cognitive processes underlying these associations.
Task-completion and learning-oriented GenAI use may not only contribute to differences in cognitive engagement but may themselves reflect students' existing tendencies to engage with academic tasks.

Students who seek to minimize cognitive effort may be more likely to adopt task-completion forms of GenAI use, whereas students who seek to engage more deeply with learning materials may preferentially use GenAI in learning-oriented ways.
Although controlling for prior academic effort partly accounts for such preexisting differences, the present study did not directly measure cognitive engagement during GenAI use.

Future research combining longitudinal designs such as this study with process measures of students' interactions with GenAI (e.g., Y. Chen et al., 2026; Pi et al., 2026) will therefore be important for distinguishing these mechanisms.

text.text: Emerging theoretical frameworks such as the SYNC model (Fan et al., 2026) may be generative for this kind of empirical work.

text.text: Further, the relatively clear pattern observed for academic effort did not extend to the other academic outcomes considered (besides value beliefs in physics).

For instance, we found no significant predictive associations of GenAI use with academic achievement across subjects and little systematic evidence that GenAI use predicted changes in students' selfconcept or value beliefs.

This pattern is noteworthy given concerns that particularly taskcompletion GenAI use may reduce opportunities for active cognitive engagement and learning and, over time, contribute to deskilling (e.g., Fan et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This pattern is noteworthy given concerns that particularly taskcompletion GenAI use may reduce opportunities for active cognitive engagement and learning and, over time, contribute to deskilling (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Fan et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">Yan et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Several explanations for this pattern are possible.
First, changes in effort may precede detectable changes in broader motivational beliefs or academic competencies.

If repeated task-completion GenAI use reduces students' investment in learning activities, its consequences for skill development may accumulate gradually and become detectable only over periods longer than the single school year examined here (see the principle of cumulative continuity; Caspi et al., 2005).
text.formatted: If repeated task-completion GenAI use reduces students' investment in learning activities, its consequences for skill development may accumulate gradually and become detectable only over periods longer than the single school year examined here (see the principle of cumulative continuity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Caspi et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Second, effects may depend strongly on the particular tasks for which GenAI is used and, especially, on whether GenAI replaces cognitive processes that are necessary for the respective learning goal.
Such task-specific effects may be difficult to detect using broad self-report measures of GenAI use and subjectlevel measures of academic outcomes.

At the same time, these explanations should be considered alongside the possibility that the detrimental consequences of students' self-directed GenAI use for broader academic outcomes are smaller and less pervasive than is sometimes assumed.

Much of the concern about cognitive offloading and deskilling is based on studies examining relatively proximal learning outcomes or experimentally induced forms of GenAI use under specific task conditions (e.g., Kosmyna et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Much of the concern about cognitive offloading and deskilling is based on studies examining relatively proximal learning outcomes or experimentally induced forms of GenAI use under specific task conditions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Kosmyna et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In naturally occurring academic contexts, students may use GenAI more selectively and flexibly, such that potentially detrimental and beneficial instances of use coexist and may partly offset one another over time.

Thus, although the present findings do not rule out negative consequences of GenAI use, they provide little evidence that students' GenAI use was associated with systematic declines in broader academic competencies or motivational beliefs over the period studied.

Longer-term studies with more fine-grained measures of when, why, and how students use GenAI are needed to determine whether detrimental effects accumulate over time or remain primarily task-and context-specific.

Turning to the reverse direction, prior academic achievement consistently predicted subsequent GenAI use across subjects, with initially higher-achieving students reporting less frequent GenAI use than lower-achieving students.
Importantly, this pattern emerged for both task-completion and learning-oriented GenAI use.
This finding only partly aligns with our hypotheses.
We had expected lower-achieving students to engage more frequently in taskcompletion GenAI use.
We had also expected higher-achieving students to engage more frequently in learning-oriented use.
Instead, higher achievement was associated with less frequent use of GenAI for both purposes.
One possible interpretation is that prior achievement primarily predicts students' overall need or propensity to seek GenAI assistance rather than the specific purposes for which they use it.
Lower-achieving students may experience greater difficulty completing academic tasks independently.

They may therefore have more reasons to turn to GenAI, both to facilitate task completion and to obtain explanations or other forms of learning support (potentially as a result of lower self-regulatory competencies; e.g., Daumiller & Dresel, 2019; Fan et al., 2026; Tankelevitch et al., 2024).
text.formatted: They may therefore have more reasons to turn to GenAI, both to facilitate task completion and to obtain explanations or other forms of learning support (potentially as a result of lower self-regulatory competencies; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Daumiller & Dresel, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Fan et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Tankelevitch et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, higher-achieving students may need less external assistance because they can more readily complete academic tasks using their existing knowledge and (self-regulatory) skills.

From this perspective, achievement may be relevant primarily to whether and how often students draw on GenAI as an academic resource, rather than to whether they use it to complete tasks or for learning.
This pattern is particularly relevant from an educational equity perspective.

Rather than demonstrating that GenAI necessarily exacerbates existing achievement differences, our findings indicate that GenAI may become a disproportionately important component of the learning environment of lower-achieving students.
This greater reliance could potentially be beneficial if GenAI provides explanations, scaffolding, or other forms of support that help students overcome difficulties (e.g., Fan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This greater reliance could potentially be beneficial if GenAI provides explanations, scaffolding, or other forms of support that help students overcome difficulties (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Fan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, it could reinforce existing differences if GenAI is used in ways that reduce engagement in learning-relevant cognitive processes or if learners use AI differently depending on their misconceptions about AI, which have been shown to vary according to cognitive and motivational variables (Jaggy et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Conversely, it could reinforce existing differences if GenAI is used in ways that reduce engagement in learning-relevant cognitive processes or if learners use AI differently depending on their misconceptions about AI, which have been shown to vary according to cognitive and motivational variables <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Jaggy et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, the present study cannot directly establish whether differential GenAI use led to widening achievement gaps over the period studied, but neither task-completion nor learning-oriented GenAI use was a statistically significant predictor of subsequent achievement across subjects.
At the same time, the finding that task-completion GenAI use predicted lower subsequent academic effort may point to a potentially relevant longer-term pathway (e.g., Fan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: At the same time, the finding that task-completion GenAI use predicted lower subsequent academic effort may point to a potentially relevant longer-term pathway (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Fan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Given that lower-achieving students also reported greater subsequent task-completion GenAI use, greater reliance on GenAI for task completion could contribute to differences in effort investment that may accumulate over longer periods (Caspi et al., 2005), although the present study cannot establish such a process.
text.formatted: Given that lower-achieving students also reported greater subsequent task-completion GenAI use, greater reliance on GenAI for task completion could contribute to differences in effort investment that may accumulate over longer periods <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Caspi et al., 2005)</ref>, although the present study cannot establish such a process.

text.text: Thus, our findings identify differential uptake of GenAI according to prior achievement and a potential effortrelated pathway through which such differences could become educationally relevant.
Future research should examine whether greater GenAI reliance among lower-achieving students ultimately reduces, maintains, or exacerbates existing educational inequalities over longer periods.
In contrast to academic achievement, associations of students' academic self-concept, value beliefs, and prior effort with subsequent GenAI use were small and inconsistent across subjects.

Thus, our findings provide little evidence that established subject-specific motivational beliefs systematically translate into different patterns of subsequent GenAI use, at least as captured by the relatively broad measures employed in the present study.

Given the absence of a consistent pattern across motivational constructs and subjects, we refrain from interpreting individual associations, which may reflect construct-or subject-specific variation rather than robust relationships between academic motivation and subsequent GenAI use.
Whether motivation becomes more relevant when GenAI use is assessed at the level of specific learning situations or decisions remains an important question for future research.

Although significant associations emerged primarily between prior GenAI use and later academic effort as well as between prior achievement and later GenAI use, we believe these findings have important educational implications.

Changes in academic effort may represent an earlier emerging process-level indicator that precedes detectable changes in academic achievement, particularly in older secondary school students whose competencies and motivational tendencies are already relatively established and who have already selected their learning environments accordingly (for example, course choices in upper secondary education; e.g., Eccles & Wigfield, 2020).

text.text: Reduced cognitive and behavioral investment during learning activities may accumulate gradually over longer periods of time before translating into measurable achievement differences.

This possibility may be especially relevant for younger learners who are still developing foundational competencies, learning strategies, and motivational tendencies (e.g., Eccles & Wigfield, 2000; Wigfield et al., 2021).

text.text: Although task-completion GenAI use was associated with lower subsequent effort in the present study, task-completion use should not necessarily be considered maladaptive in all learning situations.
Cognitive offloading can be adaptive when it frees cognitive resources for processes that are more relevant to the intended learning goal (Risko & Gilbert, 2016; Sweller, 2011).

text.text: Thus, the distinction between task-completion and learning-oriented use examined here may represent a useful but necessarily broad approximation of educationally relevant differences in GenAI use.
Ultimately, the consequences of GenAI use may depend more specifically on whether GenAI replaces cognitive activity that is necessary for the respective learning goal (e.g., Fan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Ultimately, the consequences of GenAI use may depend more specifically on whether GenAI replaces cognitive activity that is necessary for the respective learning goal (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Fan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore move toward more fine-grained conceptualizations of GenAI use that capture not only students' general purposes for using GenAI but also what cognitive work is delegated and in which learning situations.

From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that educational guidance should focus not only on whether students use GenAI, but also on how they engage with these systems (e.g., Fan et al., 2026).
text.formatted: From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that educational guidance should focus not only on whether students use GenAI, but also on how they engage with these systems (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Fan et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The associations with academic effort indicate that encouraging students to use GenAI in ways that support their own engagement with learning materials may be particularly important.
This does not necessarily imply discouraging all forms of task-completion use.

Rather, students may benefit from support in recognizing when GenAI facilitates learning and when it functions primarily as a substitute for effort and engagement that would otherwise contribute to learning.
Developing such metacognitive judgments may become an important component of GenAI literacy in the educational context (see OECD & European Commission, 2026).
text.formatted: Developing such metacognitive judgments may become an important component of GenAI literacy in the educational context (see <ref type="bibr">OECD & European Commission, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Such metacognitive support may be particularly relevant for lower-achieving students.

Across subjects, these students subsequently reported more frequent task-completion as well as learning-oriented GenAI use, suggesting that GenAI may play a comparatively larger role in their academic activities.

Lower achievement at T1 predicted higher GenAI use at T2 (after controlling for prior GenAI use at T1), which may indicate that students experiencing greater academic difficulties are more likely to turn to GenAI tools, potentially as a compensatory strategy.

This interpretation aligns with prior work suggesting that students facing high academic demands and pressure (Abbas et al., 2024), as well as those with more executive functioning challenges (Klarin et al., 2024), may turn to GenAI tools to cope with these challenges.

text.text: Our findings further align with prior experimental work (e.g., Stadler et al., 2024), which showed that GenAI tool use aimed at reducing cognitive load was associated with lower cognitive engagement during learning activities.

text.text: Extending this work, the present findings suggest that these patterns may also persist over time in authentic educational contexts.

Although greater task-completion use was not significantly associated with lower subsequent achievement in the present study, its higher prevalence among lower-achieving students and its negative association with subsequent effort warrant further investigation.
These findings do not justify recommending that lower-achieving students use GenAI less.

Instead, they suggest exploring how educational support can help especially lower-achieving students use GenAI in ways that sustain productive engagement with academic tasks, given their comparatively more frequent interactions with GenAI.

Our longitudinal data also document the rapid emergence of GenAI use among secondary school students, highlighting the increasing educational relevance of the topic in line with descriptive findings from other countries showing, for example, that more than half of U.S. teenagers have used GenAI for schoolwork (McClain et al., 2026).

text.text: In this sample, substantial increases in students' GenAI use emerged even within the relatively short time frame of a single school year, underlining how quickly GenAI tools are becoming integrated into students' academic practices.
This pattern aligns with recent reports suggesting that GenAI has already been adopted by a large proportion of secondary school and university students internationally (Unterweger et al., 2026).

text.text: Taken together, these findings empirically support educational discussions surrounding GenAI in moving beyond binary questions of whether students should use GenAI tools and instead focusing more strongly on how these systems are used during learning (Giannakos et al., 2025; Panadero & Broadbent, 2025; Xiao et al., 2026; Yan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Taken together, these findings empirically support educational discussions surrounding GenAI in moving beyond binary questions of whether students should use GenAI tools and instead focusing more strongly on how these systems are used during learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Giannakos et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Panadero & Broadbent, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Xiao et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Yan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Educational guidance and GenAI literacy efforts may therefore need to emphasize forms of GenAI use that encourage explanation, reflection, revision, and active problem solving rather than uses primarily aimed at minimizing effort or rapidly completing tasks.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings of the present study: First, the measures assessing students' Gen AI use were not subject-specific, whereas academic achievement, motivation, and effort were assessed separately across school subjects.

Thus, although it could be argued that if students use GenAI tools, they may use them similarly across multiple academic subjects, we were not able to formally account for differential GenAI use patterns across subjects.
For example, students may rely on GenAI differently in subjects in which they perceive themselves as less competent or experience lower intrinsic interest (e.g., Jansen et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For example, students may rely on GenAI differently in subjects in which they perceive themselves as less competent or experience lower intrinsic interest (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Jansen et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: To partially address this issue, we conducted all analyses separately for each subject and controlled for the respective T1 measures.

This approach ensures that the associations (i.e., between prior GenAI use and later academic outcomes as well as between prior academic outcomes and later GenAI use) are estimated by comparing students who are similar on the other variables at baseline.
Nevertheless, the present study cannot fully determine whether the observed associations differ systematically across subject-specific contexts.
Second, the measurement and conceptualization of task-completion and learningoriented GenAI use are rather broad.

Moreover, the two factors were strongly correlated within each time point, so the divergent effort findings rest on comparatively limited variation distinguishing the two forms of use and should be replicated with items designed to separate the two purposes more clearly.

Although distinguishing between these two purposes provides a useful first approximation of how students engage with GenAI, the same form of GenAI use may have different implications depending on the specific task and learning context.
In particular, task-completion GenAI use should not necessarily be understood as maladaptive or detrimental to learning.
Offloading a specific subtask to GenAI may sometimes allow learners to allocate their cognitive resources more effectively to aspects of a task that are more relevant to the intended learning goal.
Third, although the theoretical framework of the present study centers on differences in active cognitive engagement with academic tasks, cognitive engagement itself was not measured directly.
Instead, the study distinguished forms of GenAI use theorized to reflect differing levels of cognitive engagement during learning activities.

Although this approach is grounded in educational psychology theory and consistent with emerging empirical findings on GenAI-supported cognitive offloading, the present data cannot directly verify the underlying cognitive processes through which these associations emerge.

Future research should therefore assess GenAI use at a more fine-grained, situational level, capturing which strategies students employ for which components of a task and under what circumstances, including examinations of the role of cognitive engagement in these contexts.

Such approaches could move beyond a general distinction between task-completion and learningoriented use toward identifying when and for which learning goals particular forms of GenAI use constitute adaptive and strategically appropriate tool use.

Finally, although the longitudinal design strengthens the interpretation of temporal associations, the assumptions required for causal interpretations (Angrist & Pischke, 2009) are strong and may not fully hold in practice.

text.text: One particular advantage of our cross-lagged panel design is that longitudinal information is available for all variables whose associations we examined: we thus modeled associations between GenAI use at T1 and academic outcomes at T2 while controlling for the academic outcomes at T1.
Controlling for prior measures of the outcome has been argued to strengthen causal inference from longitudinal observational data (VanderWeele et al., 2020).

text.text: GenAI is rapidly becoming part of students' everyday learning environments, yet the antecedents and consequences of secondary school students' self-directed GenAI use remain poorly understood.
Across one school year, task-completion GenAI use tended to predict lower subsequent effort, whereas learning-oriented use showed more positive associations with subsequent effort.
At the same time, lower-achieving students reported more frequent subsequent GenAI use across subjects, whereas prior GenAI use was not significantly associated with later achievement.
Rather than being uniformly beneficial or harmful, the consequences of GenAI use likely depend on when, why, and how students use it.
Educational guidance should therefore move beyond simply promoting or restricting GenAI use and instead help students use it strategically to support sustained effort.
Identifying how these patterns develop, and for whom they are beneficial or detrimental, will be important for supporting learning in increasingly AI-rich educational environments.

Our findings suggest that lower-achieving students in particular, given their comparatively more frequent use, might benefit from interventions supporting GenAI use in ways that sustain productive engagement with academic tasks.
